title: Bessent to AI CEOs: 'alarmism without solutions is not leadership'
subtitle: On Axios, the Treasury Secretary compared executives who warn of catastrophe while asking for federal rules to Hannibal Lecter — and ruled out a liability shield.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on The Axios Show taped October 3, dismissed calls from Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk to slow advanced-model development as 'alarmism without solutions.' Asked whether frontier labs should voluntarily pause, Bessent's reply was direct: 'Well, then they should slow down.' He compared executives who publicly warn about catastrophic risk while simultaneously asking the federal government for regulation to Hannibal Lecter — 'stop me before I kill again' — and made clear the administration will not act as a liability shield.

The specific line that matters for the legal posture: the federal government cannot absolve frontier labs of responsibility and take it on itself. That rules out, by name, the structure some frontier labs had privately floated — a federal framework that preempts state tort claims in exchange for federal licensing. The September round of CEO warnings, plus Bill Gates's 'billion deaths' comment, had been read in Washington as groundwork for exactly that trade. Treasury has now closed that door publicly.

The remarks dovetail with the broader administration posture: the Trump White House's 'Super Intelligence Accord' from September 30 explicitly asks the six largest labs to self-police, and Michael Kratsios has pushed the 'Carolina Principles' at G20 as an alternative to EU-style technology-specific regulation. The Bessent intervention locks in the political cost of that approach — labs cannot both claim catastrophic risk and shed liability — and raises the stakes for the FTC investigations into OpenAI and Anthropic announced earlier this month.

A takeaway for learners: 'alarmism without solutions' is a political test, not just a soundbite. If you work on AI policy, assume the next six months will reward specific, implementable proposals — compute thresholds, mandatory evaluations, incident-disclosure timelines, model-weight security standards — and penalize abstract existential-risk framing. The gap between 'this is dangerous' and 'here is the exact clause of the exact statute that fixes it' is where the serious policy work now lives.
